common_name: Choptank River Belle Azalea (Fragrant White Pink-Blush Coastal Azalea Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained sandy soil in part shade; Choptank River Belle is a named selection of the dwarf, suckering Coastal Azalea chosen for an especially heavy flush of fragrant bicolor flowers.

directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, humus-rich, acidic, sandy soil in part shade, recreating the open coastal-plain pine woodland where its parent species grows wild. Choptank River Belle is a named selection of Rhododendron atlanticum (Coastal Azalea) chosen for its very fragrant, white, pink-blushed flowers to about 1.5 inches across, opening in mid-spring on a low, suckering shrub that spreads gradually into loose colonies rather than staying as a single tidy specimen. Like the species, it tolerates drier, sandier soils than most streambank native azaleas once established, making it a good low woodland-edge or naturalized planting for part-shade borders. Prune only to remove dead wood, since little shaping is needed to keep it looking at home in an informal native planting.

common_name: Aphrodite Azalea (Rosy Purplish-Pink Glenn Dale Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Aphrodite is a Glenn Dale Hybrid grown for abundant, rosy purplish-pink spring flowers on a cold-hardier plant than the tender Southern Indian Hybrids.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Aphrodite is a Glenn Dale Hybrid azalea from the breeding program USDA horticulturist Benjamin Yeo Morrison ran at the Glenn Dale Plant Introduction Station in Maryland from the 1930s through the 1950s, a program built to combine the cold hardiness of Korean and Japanese azalea species with the large flowers of tender Asian forms. Its single, rosy to light purplish-pink flowers open to roughly 2 inches wide and are produced in such abundance that the plant can be smothered in bloom at peak flush. The shrub forms an upright, well-branched, semi-evergreen to evergreen mound 3-5 feet tall and wide, flowering in mid-spring alongside many other Glenn Dale selections. Water deeply during dry spells, keep a mulch layer over the shallow root zone, and prune only right after bloom since next year's flower buds set soon afterward.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Glenn Dale Hybrid Documentation

common_name: Buccaneer Azalea (Brilliant Orange-Red Glenn Dale Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Buccaneer is a Glenn Dale Hybrid widely regarded as one of the best orange-red cultivars the program produced.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Buccaneer is a Glenn Dale Hybrid azalea bred by Benjamin Yeo Morrison at the Glenn Dale Plant Introduction Station and is consistently ranked among the standout selections of the group for its brilliant, large, funnel-shaped orange-red flowers marked with a darker brick-red flare on the upper lobe. The display is vivid enough to anchor a planting on its own, opening in mid-to-late spring on a vigorous, well-branched, semi-evergreen to evergreen shrub that reaches 3-5 feet tall and wide. As with other Glenn Dale selections, the bloom comes in one heavy flush rather than repeating through the season. Water deeply during dry spells, mulch to keep the root zone cool and moist, and prune only right after flowering since next year's buds form soon after bloom ends.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Glenn Dale Hybrid Documentation

common_name: Geisha Azalea (Purplish-Pink Striped Glenn Dale Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Geisha is a mid-season Glenn Dale Hybrid valued for its intense purplish-pink, lighter-centered striped flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Geisha is a Glenn Dale Hybrid azalea from Benjamin Yeo Morrison's USDA breeding program, producing mid-season flowers up to 2.5 inches across in an intense purplish-pink with a lighter, almost white center and fine striping through each petal, a pattern similar to the related cultivar 'Festive' but leaning more purple than red. The shrub grows into an upright, well-branched, semi-evergreen to evergreen mound 3-5 feet tall and wide, carrying its single heavy bloom flush in mid-spring. Its patterned flowers make it a popular choice among collectors assembling a range of Glenn Dale bicolor and striped forms. Water deeply during dry spells, mulch over the shallow root zone, and prune only right after bloom since next year's flower buds set soon afterward.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Glenn Dale Hybrid Documentation

common_name: Pink Pearl Azalea (Hose-in-Hose White-to-Salmon-Pink Kurume Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.5) soil in partial shade; Pink Pearl is one of plant explorer E.H. Wilson's early-twentieth-century Kurume introductions, grown for its soft multicolor hose-in-hose flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.5) soil in partial shade. Pink Pearl is one of the Kurume azalea cultivars brought out of Japan in the early twentieth century by plant explorer E.H. Wilson as part of the group later known as Wilson's Fifty, and it remains prized for its multicolored hose-in-hose (double-within-double) flowers, which open white at the center and shade through soft pink to a deeper, ruffled salmon-pink at the petal edges, with slender white stamens extending gracefully beyond the bloom. The small, glossy, fine-textured leaves and compact mounding habit are typical of Kurume azaleas, producing a dense cover of flowers in spring that can obscure the foliage entirely at peak bloom. Strongly acidic, humus-rich soil and consistent moisture are essential, since chlorosis from insufficient soil acidity is the most common cultural problem. Prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since next year's buds form soon after bloom ends.

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.5) soil in partial shade; Suetsumuhana, sold in the West under the trade name 'Flame', is one of E.H. Wilson's early-twentieth-century Kurume introductions prized for its single reddish-pink flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.5) soil in partial shade. Suetsumuhana is one of the original Kurume azalea clones E.H. Wilson brought from Japan to Western gardens in the early twentieth century, where it was given the English trade name 'Flame' to distinguish it from the native deciduous Flame Azalea (Rhododendron calendulaceum), an entirely different species. Its single, reddish-pink flowers cover the plant in a dense spring flush typical of Kurume cultivars, set against small, glossy, fine-textured evergreen leaves on a compact, naturally mounding shrub. Strongly acidic, evenly moist, humus-rich soil is essential for good performance and for avoiding the iron chlorosis that affects azaleas grown in alkaline ground. Prune only lightly right after flowering if shaping is wanted, since next year's flower buds set soon after the spring bloom ends.

common_name: Apple Blossom Azalea (Pale Pink White-Throated Kurume Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.5) soil in partial shade; Apple Blossom is one of E.H. Wilson's original early-twentieth-century Kurume introductions, grown for its soft pale pink, white-throated hose-in-hose flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.5) soil in partial shade. Apple Blossom is one of the original Kurume azalea clones introduced from Japan by plant explorer E.H. Wilson in the late 1910s as part of the group later catalogued as Wilson's Fifty, and it takes its name from its soft, pale pink, hose-in-hose flowers with a clear white throat, reminiscent of the color of apple blossom petals. The small, glossy, fine-textured evergreen leaves and tight, naturally rounded habit are classic Kurume traits, and the spring bloom is dense enough to cover the plant in flower. Strongly acidic, evenly moist, humus-rich soil is essential for good color and vigor and to avoid the iron chlorosis that affects azaleas in alkaline ground. Prune only lightly right after flowering if shaping is wanted, since next year's buds form soon after bloom ends.

common_name: Osakazuki Azalea (Large-Flowered Hot Pink Satsuki Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Osakazuki is a traditional Satsuki azalea cultivar grown for its large, single, hot pink flowers with darker red touches.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching well to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Osakazuki is a long-established Satsuki azalea cultivar from Japan's centuries-old tradition of Satsuki breeding, valued for its large, single flowers in a hot pink shaded with touches of deeper red, set against small, glossy green leaves. Like other Satsuki selections, it blooms several weeks later than most Southern Indica and Kurume azaleas, typically in late spring to early summer, extending the azalea season in the garden. Its compact, twiggy growth and tolerance of heavy pruning also make it a popular subject for bonsai training in addition to container and border use. Water deeply during dry spells and prune only right after flowering, since this later-flowering type sets its buds for the following year soon after bloom ends.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Nikko is an ultra-dwarf Satsuki azalea cultivar popular for bonsai as well as small-scale container and border planting.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, keeping the shallow root system mulched and evenly moist. Nikko is an ultra-dwarf Satsuki azalea cultivar from Japan's long tradition of Satsuki breeding, with small, variable flowers ranging from pale to darker peach-pink, often gently variegated and set off by a greenish throat. Its naturally tiny leaves, slow growth, and fine branching have made it one of the most widely used Satsuki cultivars for bonsai training, though it also performs well as a small-scale rock garden or container specimen. Like other Satsuki cultivars, it blooms later in the season than most Kurume and Southern Indica azaleas, typically in late spring to early summer. Water deeply during dry spells and prune only right after flowering if shaping is needed, since next year's buds set soon after this later bloom period ends.

common_name: Kogetsu Azalea (White Red-Variegated Sokojiro Satsuki Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Kogetsu is a traditional Satsuki azalea cultivar noted for its white flowers marked with dramatic red variegation.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching well to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Kogetsu is a traditional Satsuki azalea cultivar prized for its white flowers streaked and flared with vivid red variegation, often in the striking sokojiro pattern where red petals carry a white center, each bloom made more elegant by its classic rounded petal form. As with other Satsuki cultivars, flowering comes several weeks later than most Kurume and Southern Indica azaleas, typically in late spring to early summer, and the compact, twiggy growth responds well to the heavy pruning used in bonsai training as well as ordinary border and container culture. Water deeply during dry spells and prune only right after flowering if shaping is needed, since this later-flowering type sets its buds for next year soon after bloom ends.
